articles.title_orig: The 2026 iPad Mini is a terrific tiny tablet — for a big price
articles.title_zh: The 2026 iPad Mini is a terrific tiny tablet — for a big price
articles.content_orig:
With better performance and a better screen, this is a Mini to be reckoned with. But it’s not perfect, and it sure isn’t cheap.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
With better performance and a better screen, this is a Mini to be reckoned with. But it’s not perfect, and it sure isn’t cheap.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
The iPad Mini sometimes feels like a trap. It is, in some ways and for some people, the perfect iPad: meaningfully larger than my phone’s screen but still small and light enough to use for reading in bed or gaming on the subway. As most of the rest of the iPad line has tilted ever closer to laptop territory, the Mini might be the most iPad-y iPad left. I’ve taken a Mini everywhere with me since the very first one. But Apple only updates the Mini sporadically, and those updates sometimes feel like someone inside Apple Park picked its specs by closing their eyes and clicking randomly in an Excel sheet. The Mini is always a little underpowered, a little overpriced, and a little afield in Apple’s tablet lineup. We, the iPad Mini People, sometimes feel a little forgotten.
This year’s model , though, is an upgrade through and through. Apple made the screen larger and better, while making the iPad itself smaller and lighter. It upgraded the processor in a big way. It made the whole package more durable, so you can take it to more places and use it for more things. It actually feels like a tablet made for a reason, not just another occasional bone thrown to the small-tablet fans.
For the past week, I’ve been testing the midnight iPad Mini with cell service, 512GB of storage, and the nano-texture matte display coating. I really like it. It’s the best iPad Mini yet, and a huge leap over the previous model . The one in my hands also costs $1,249, and I cannot in good conscience tell you to buy it. Even the very cheapest version — Wi-Fi only, 128GB of storage, regular OLED display — starts at $699, by a wide margin the highest starting price ever for a Mini.
If you don’t already know the iPad Mini is your one true love, there’s probably a better iPad out there for you. But if you’re an iPad Mini Person and you can stomach the price? You’re getting the best Mini in years.
The Mini’s new display is its most important and most controversial upgrade. It now measures 8.5 inches instead of 8.3, and it’s now a 2316 x 1512 OLED panel instead of an LCD. The OLED gives the screen a little more dynamic range than the previous model, with brighter bright spots and darker dark spots. Its peak brightness is noticeably brighter than before, and its minimum brightness is low enough to be totally pleasant for reading in the dark (as long as you’re in dark mode). In general, it’s just a little more crisp and contrast-y, in a nice way; the old Mini’s display was the least of my worries, but the OLED is a solid improvement. The tablet I tested also has Apple’s nano-texture matte finish , which seems to dull and darken the screen slightly; on a particularly white background, the whole thing seems to shimmer. I suspect I’d like the OLED panel even more without it.
The nano-texture does, however, do an excellent job of reducing glare. The effect is actually really cool: The textured coating doesn’t extend to the bezels, so you can see a source of light or glare come in from the edge of the screen and then simply disappear as it hits the screen. So what you lose in pure screen fidelity, you gain in the ability to read on the iPad in a coffee shop without it reflecting the overhead lights like a mirror. The nano-texture option costs an extra $100, though, and requires you to upgrade to 256GB of storage, so you’re now looking at a $900 tablet. Spend the extra money on the cellular version or, better yet, don’t spend it at all.
For some reason, Apple has never deigned to put its ProMotion display tech on the iPad Mini, which has a refresh rate capped at 60Hz rather than the 120Hz you’ll get on most other recent Apple devices. This is such an odd spec choice that it has launched a bunch of conspiracy theories. Maybe it’s to make more people buy an iPhone Duo instead? Maybe it’s a 120Hz panel downgraded to 60Hz by software just to make people upgrade again next time? Apple’s answer, to Chris Lawley and others, has been something to the effect of “120Hz is irrelevant, OLED’s faster pixel response solves the problems.” I don’t agree. I don’t think the lack of ProMotion is an immediate and total dealbreaker, but refresh rates matter ! To games and high-touch creative apps, of course, but you notice the difference even with basic swiping and zooming. The Apple Pencil feels more juddery moving across my screen. On a 120Hz screen, I can scroll a browser page and still clearly read the text as it’s moving. With 60Hz, it gets blurry. In all these cases, even if you don’t explicitly see the difference, you really do feel it.
The most meaningful upgrade in the new Mini, at least for me and how I use my iPad, is that it is designed to be more or less waterproof and dustproof. Its IP67 rating means that the Mini got the highest possible score for protection from “solid foreign objects,” which for our purposes mostly just means dust won’t get inside, and is also “protected against the effects of temporary immersion in water.” It’s not quite as rugged as, say, the iPhone 18 Pro, and I don’t recommend using it as an underwater camera or anything, but your tablet should be fine as long as you don’t drop it in the tub and leave it for a while.
This increased ruggedness immediately changed my iPad usage in a couple of ways. I became less worried about handing the Mini to my toddler, whose general stickiness and penchant for spilling things no longer feel like threats. I also started using the Mini more in the kitchen — I love to cook with an iPad nearby for recipes and Community episodes, and it was nice not to be constantly guarding against flour explosions and water spills. At one point, the iPad Mini even came with me in the shower during a particularly close football game. It’s still kicking.
This is, for lack of a better word, the Field iPad.
The Mini’s IP rating is also the feature that finally made me see who Apple sees as the ideal iPad Mini user. This is, for lack of a better word, the Field iPad. We hear all the time about pilots who use Minis instead of sheaves of paperwork, but Apple also sees them in use on construction sites, oil rigs, doctor’s offices, and all kinds of other places. (It’s a fun rabbit hole, actually — can I interest you in an “explosion proof” last-gen Mini for $4,500 or so?) Apple’s goal with the Mini is not really to maximize performance, satisfy the pixel-peepers, or enhance creator workflows. It’s durability and usability. Body and screen.
Apple made a couple of changes to the Mini to receive its IP rating, like ditching the speaker holes and opting for what it calls an Acoustic Display. It means the sound fires out of the front panel rather than from speaker holes. (Some TVs currently work the same way.) It doesn’t sound any better than before, maybe a tiny bit bassier, but it also doesn’t sound worse, and if anything it’s slightly better to have the sound actually pointed at you instead of out the sides of the tablet. Mostly it’s a wash in service of the ruggedization, which is good enough for me.
The rest of the hardware is just wins all the way around. The A20 Pro chip, the chipset also on the iPhone 18 Pro (and the Duo ), benchmarks about 50 percent faster than the 2024 Mini for standard computing tasks, and about three times as fast for graphics-intensive ones. (The chip in my review unit has one more CPU core than the A20 Pro in the cheaper Minis; those will still be drastic improvements, but maybe a hair less so.) I notice the difference, even side by side with the old model, in how fast apps load and games play. Games like Assas

articles.title_orig: Detentions, resignations, probes shake Serbia after students toppled strongman Vucic in election
articles.title_zh: Detentions, resignations, probes shake Serbia after students toppled strongman Vucic in election
articles.content_orig:
I was wrong. Until October 25, when Serbia’s students won an extraordinary victory in an early general election, I thought they had little chance of bringing down Aleksandar Vučić, their country’s authoritarian leader. For the last two years I had followed as the students created a leaderless movement and selected candidates for an electoral list to run against Vučić and his party in a vote that he had called. All this was interesting, I thought. But Serbia was constantly witnessing bouts of protest, and it seemed hard to imagine that such a broad-church movement—one that sought to unite conservative and religious nationalists, left-wing liberals, and everyone in between—could unseat a party that had the power to give pensioners a bonus payment just before an election, compel public-sector workers to cast ballots for it at the risk of losing their jobs, or pay people for images of their ballot slip with the right name circled.
And yet the students won, not narrowly but by a crushing margin. After the Serbs toppled their wartime leader Slobodan Milošević, in October 2000, Georgians, Ukrainians, Egyptians, and others seeking to bring down their own dictators and autocrats studied the Serbian case or received training in how to do so from a Belgrade organization that claims to have worked in fifty-two countries since then. Now that young people are taking to the streets in France, India, and Albania, following a year of youth protests in countries as diverse as Nepal and Madagascar, I think we can bet that the demand for Serbs as consultants and trainers in unconventional methods of leader-toppling will boom again.
The current wave of student protest in Serbia began on November 1, 2024, when a recently renovated canopy at Novi Sad station collapsed and killed sixteen people. Corruption was alleged, along with official neglect. On November 22 students and professors who had gathered for a memorial to the victims at Belgrade University’s Faculty of Dramatic Arts were assaulted by thugs, probably paid for or linked to Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS). The attack galvanized students across the country, who now took the lead in organizing protests and vigils and shutting down classes.
So far, so routine. Vučić, a minister under Milošević, and his party had been in power since 2012, and every year for the last decade there have been protests for one reason or another—against plans for lithium mining, plans to develop Belgrade’s waterfront, plans for Jared Kushner to develop the NATO-bombed former General Staff building in Belgrade into a luxury hotel, and so on. Over the years these had few if any results. But in the aftermath of the Novi Sad disaster the government appeared rattled and apprehensive.
Over the winter the protests grew smaller but did not fizzle out. Then, on March 15, 2025, some 300,000 people gathered to protest in Belgrade. Independent media called it the largest-ever protest in Serbian history. During the protest there was a sudden panic and many began to flee. Independent outlets quickly reported that the police had used a crowd-control “sound cannon” known as a Long Range Acoustic Device. According to the student movement’s manifesto, the sounds they heard and the “shockwave” caused the crowd to scatter: “civil society organizations collected over 3,000 testimonies from people describing the same moment and the physical distress that followed.” The authorities denied the use of the sound canon, which would have been illegal. This only enraged and energized the movement more. To publicize the cause, one group of students cycled to Strasbourg; another ran 1,200 miles to Brussels. Pro-Vučić thugs continued to attack protesters in bouts of violence, and the pro-government media more or less ignored what was happening. But the students kept going.
In November 2025 thousands of demonstrators turned out in Belgrade to protest a new law speeding along Kushner’s hotel development. The following month Kushner pulled out of the scheme after Serbia’s prosecutor for organized crime charged the minister of culture, among others, with falsifying documents in order to revoke the building’s status as a protected cultural monument. That such a thing could happen to a minister showed that things were already beginning to change, I was told by Slobodan Markovich, a historian at Belgrade University who is close to the student movement.
Much of middle-class, educated Serbia loathes Vučić and his party. In classic Balkan mode, the SNS is a vast patronage machine: until now many jobs in the public sector depended on membership. Much of the judiciary and media fell under party control, too. Ivan Vejvoda, a political scientist who began demonstrating as a student in 1968 and has witnessed or participated in many of the major events in Serbia’s history ever since, summed it up in a recent essay . Under Vučić, he wrote, “people lived for years in a captured state where they witnessed corruption, nepotism and clientelism every day.”
At the same time, he noted, organized crime has been “laundering enormous amounts of money” in the construction business, which offers easy opportunities to clean dirty funds. Much research has been done to reveal the link between Balkan drug trafficking groups and the construction boom of the last few years. In 2015 Darko Šarić, the head of a notorious international cocaine smuggling gang, was jailed. At a subsequent trial for money laundering the court heard how the group would, according to the judgement, invest their money in real estate, among other things. It was no surprise that the students’ main slogan this election was “Serbia or the Mafia.”
Vučić’s was not a dictatorship that murdered its opponents or threw them in jail for years. Its rule has been much more subtle. The journalist Jelena Petković told me how, in 2018, she was slowly but surely pushed out of her newspaper when it started falling in line with the regime, not least by simply ignoring stories that editors knew would annoy Vučić and the party. Zoran Kusovac, another journalist, told me a revealing anecdote. He asked an old friend of his why she had divorced her husband, who had a high-ranking job at a major government-supporting TV channel. “The main reason,” she said, was that every night, “as we were lying in bed, Vučić called to analyze the evening news bulletin and what was good and what was not good and what he wanted for tomorrow.”
February 15 is Serbian Statehood Day. It celebrates the moment in 1835 when Serbian leaders and several thousand prominent men and village heads from across the country adopted its first constitution in Kragujevac, seventy miles south of Belgrade. The death of Yugoslavia devastated that town, the home of a car and arms maker called Zastava. Things are much improved nowadays. Fiat builds cars in a modern plant there and Serbia exports arms around the world, including to Israel and Ukraine.
At a rally the students convened in Kragujevac to mark the day this year, I met a history student named Katarina Draganovic. I said that the energy seemed to be draining from the protests after fifteen months. “It is not about demonstrations anymore,” she replied. Students were fanning out across the country now, going to every town and village, and asking people “about their problems and what they want us to focus on when we win.”
In some ninety university and higher education departments, student “plenums” were debating ideas and selecting experts from among academics, medics, engineers, farmers, actors, and others. The movement had first called for an early general election in May 2025, and by December they had started collecting signatures on a petition for one. Eventually the students would select 250 of the experts to be on their list of candidates for parliament—what would be called the Student List. None of these experts had political backgrounds. Nor, however, were any of them students. The movement eschewed the idea of having any

articles.title_orig: Saudi Aramco Profit Jumps Despite Damaging Attacks on Pipelines and Refineries
articles.title_zh: Saudi Aramco Profit Jumps Despite Damaging Attacks on Pipelines and Refineries
articles.content_orig:
Aramco reported a 9% rise in third-quarter adjusted net income on Tuesday on stronger refining margins.
The Saudi oil giant posted adjusted net income of $31.2 billion for the quarter, up from $28.6 billion a year earlier. The figure exceeded the median analyst consensus estimate of $30.66 billion, according to the company.
Aramco's downstream business, which processes crude oil into fuels and other products, posted adjusted earnings before interest and taxes of $10.3 billion, up 234% from a year earlier, driven by stronger refining margins.
"Geopolitical uncertainty and attacks on key energy facilities continued to amplify the global energy supply crisis in the third quarter of 2026, with serious implications for global energy security," Aramco CEO Amin H. Nasser said in a statement.
Nasser said the company's operational flexibility and supply network enabled it to continue delivering energy to customers despite the disruptions. Aramco is also exploring additional overseas storage capacity and alternative export routes to strengthen its global supply network.
The company generated $28.2 billion in free cash flow during the quarter, up from $23.6 billion a year earlier.
Aramco said its board declared a third-quarter base dividend of $21.9 billion, up 3.5% year on year, to be paid in the fourth quarter.
The company also said its major upstream projects remained on track and highlighted its acquisition of a 49% stake in Saudi artificial intelligence company HUMAIN.
– CNBC's Emma Graham contributed to this story.

articles.title_orig: Europe on alert after supermarket freezers hit by cyber-attacks in 10 countries
articles.title_zh: Europe on alert after supermarket freezers hit by cyber-attacks in 10 countries
articles.content_orig:
A spate of cyber-attacks that hit supermarket chains across at least 10 European countries on Monday has prompted European Union officials to warn of a deliberate attempt to disrupt the food supply chain.
Supermarkets have reported problems in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Germany and Sweden, and the significant increase in freezer temperatures has forced retailers to discard food.
Temperatures in chains across Europe reportedly rose as high as 50C (122F).
No-one has yet admitted carrying out the cyber-attacks.
The European Union has raised concerns about the attacks, which come three weeks after a cyber-attack disrupted as many as 700 French grocery stores, causing food losses estimated at tens of millions of euros.
The security of refrigeration systems as well as other devices that can be monitored remotely has heightened concerns about government-backed hybrid attacks.
The EU's food and agriculture commissioner, Christophe Hansen, said the bloc was taking the incidents very seriously and warned of further disruption in the future.
Commission spokesman Thomas Regnier was careful not to attribute blame, but said: "These incidents of course show once again how cyber-attacks can disrupt essential services and affect citizens' daily lives."
"These are not isolated incidents and of course we have to be collectively resilient and prepared for such cyber incidents."
In Italy , Giorgia Meloni's government called a meeting with intelligence chiefs, but said the impact was "currently very limited" and most of the food distribution chain had up-to-date security systems able to fend off such attacks.
At least four Co-op supermarkets in Sicily and one business in Tuscany were affected, according to the national cybersecurity agency.
Meloni's office said those businesses affected were "mostly still equipped with obsolete security systems, with interfaces directly exposed to the internet and inadequate authentication mechanisms".
Belgian supermarkets were among those hardest-hit, with dozens of stores reporting refrigeration failures. Federal prosecutors have opened an investigation.
Mathieu Tilman, a manager at a Delhaize supermarket in Belgium, said he was shocked by this kind of attack: "I don't even understand how anyone could do this... How can we end up throwing away so much food? I find it truly distressing. In moments like these, you just feel like quitting your job."
In Ireland , 13 SuperValu stores were impacted by what the chain's owner, Musgrave Group, called a cyber-incident. "Replenishment of chilled and frozen ranges in the affected stores is well under way," a spokesman said on Monday.
A small number of corner shops in the Netherlands also suffered disruption. Last month, supermarket chain Albert Heijn had to take several services offline because of a separate cyber-attack.
There was disruption to refrigeration systems at the Rewe Büsken supermarket in western Germany after a cyber-attack on system provider Danfoss, the company told the BBC. Its systems have been back in operation since Monday afternoon.
In Portugal , the Mosqueteiros group said that incidents at seven Intermarché stores had been linked to a cyberattack, which "appears to have targeted an external service provider responsible for managing the refrigeration systems".
Swedish chain ICA also said "a limited number" of its stores had experienced refrigeration problems, without confirming a cyber-attack, and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident.
In Finland , irregular temperatures were detected in a few smaller grocery stores belonging to the Kesko group, which said it was investigating the issue.
In Estonia , at least one supermarket was attacked by hackers who raised the temperature in the refrigeration units to 50C, public broadcaster ERR reported.
In the UK , the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has warned British retailers to update the software on fridge temperature controls.
The agency said the country was likely to suffer an AI-powered cyber-attack on critical national infrastructure within two years.
Richard Horne, the head of the National Cyber Security Centre, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme there were a couple of instances in the UK where "vulnerable technology has been exploited" after the cyber-attacks.
"We don't know the full impact, but we do know there are a couple of instances where vulnerable technology has been exploited and we're working with those organisations."
Asked if there was any evidence that supermarkets in Britain or freezers of the same make or model had been targeted, Horne said: "It's not just supermarkets, it's through the whole food supply chain, and we've been working through the night alerting organisations where we can see they've got exposed technology that's vulnerable in this way."

articles.title_orig: UK will face AI cyberattacks on critical infrastructure by 2028, official says
articles.title_zh: UK will face AI cyberattacks on critical infrastructure by 2028, official says
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
The U.K. will likely face artificial intelligence cyberattacks on its critical infrastructure by 2028 as criminals and states, including China and Russia , increasingly use AI in their cyber activity, Britain 's cyber chief warned Tuesday.
That could include AI-powered malware for ransomware attacks as the technology will allow “vulnerabilities that have been tolerated for far too long” to be discovered and exploited “at a scale that was once unimaginable,” Richard Horne, the head of the U.K.'s National Cyber Security Center said.
In a speech marking the publication of the NCSC's annual cyber report, Horne said the leaders of businesses and organizations of all sizes who have "got away with tech on the cheap" will have to explain why “food isn't on the shelves, lights aren't on, businesses have gone under,” if they fail to invest in cybersecurity or update out-of-date technology.
Chinese cyber activity is the “most sophisticated and sustained cyber challenge facing the U.K.” while both Russia and China will routinely use AI to achieve their geopolitical goals, the report said. Russia is intentionally conducting cyber campaigns which fall below the threshold of armed conflict while Iran is carrying out attacks against the U.K. and targeting individuals who are a threat to the Iranian regime, Horne said.
The use of AI by states and criminals is highly likely to increase the scale and efficiency of hostile operations, but AI is more likely to be used to enhance and scale existing tactics and techniques rather than find brand new vulnerabilities, the report said.
Last week, governments and corporations worked on urgent security updates after the AI-assisted discovery of vulnerabilities in a programming language vital to 70% of websites globally. The two critical flaws identified by AI could allow bad actors to get unauthenticated access to sites which, in theory, could allow them to control a web server remotely without needing a password.
Technology “underpins the automation of physical processes that are vital to modern life,” Horne said. That includes, he said, electricity switching, sluice gates in water facilities, dam operations, manufacturing lines, heating and refrigeration controls. The recent cyberattacks on refrigeration systems in French supermarkets showed how easily hostile actors could exploit civilian infrastructure, Horne said.
Russia has already attacked critical infrastructure in Europe, according to the U.K. and EU member states that said Russia's FSB security service was behind an attack on Poland's energy grid in December 2025. If the attack had been successful, 500,000 people could have lost electricity during winter.
In the U.K., malicious cyber activity is costing organizations almost $20 billion every year, the NCSC said. In 2025, the carmaker Jaguar Land Rover suffered more than $260 million in direct losses following a cyberattack which also hit suppliers and dented the U.K. economy.
“We need every organization in the UK to take action now. Not only to protect their customers, services and livelihoods, but because cybersecurity is now part of the front line defense of our nation,” said Anne Keast-Butler, director of GCHQ, Britain’s signals intelligence agency, which the NCSC is part of.
That includes implementing basic but effective cybersecurity measures such as making sure devices are up to date, limiting administrator access to systems and backing up important files and data, the NCSC said.

articles.title_orig: Russia confirms new Ukraine peace talks as Melania Trump prepares to host ceasefire meeting
articles.title_zh: Russia confirms new Ukraine peace talks as Melania Trump prepares to host ceasefire meeting
articles.content_orig:
Russia on Tuesday confirmed that peace talks with Ukraine and the U.S. will go ahead next week in Abu Dhabi, while also signaling that a meeting between Presidents Vladimir Putin , Donald Trump and Xi Jinping to end the conflict was on the table.
Putin aide Vladimir ​Medinsky will serve ⁠as Moscow's chief negotiator ​at the talks in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11, Kremlin spokesman ​Dmitry Peskov told reporters on a conference call, according to Reuters.
Separately, First Lady Melania Trump will bring Russian and Ukrainian representatives to the White House to discuss the local ceasefire in Kherson, the White House said Tuesday.
Monday saw the end of a six-day ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky and surrounding areas in the Kherson region to allow for evacuation of residents, in a pause of hostilities that the White House said was brokered by the first lady.
Ukraine on Monday accused Russia of using the ceasefire to reinforce its military positions in the city.
The first lady's summit on Thursday will be "an extraordinary moment in American history," the White House said, but did not name the representatives who will attend. Melania Trump will deliver remarks on the Oleshky ceasefire at 11 a.m. ET Thursday, it added.
Peskov also said Tuesday the Kremlin hopes to finalize plans for a trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, the U.S., and China in the coming days. The comments follow earlier reports that these countries were planning to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine, without Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the table.
Zelenskyy has said that any negotiations over Ukraine's future must include Kyiv.
"It can be acceptable only when we are at the table of negotiations," he said on Oct. 20, adding that he had discussed the proposal of a three-way meeting between the U.S., China, and Russia to negotiate an end to the nearly five-year full-scale war. "Nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine," he said.
Tensions between the U.S. and Ukraine have mounted over recent weeks amid continued strikes between Moscow and Kyiv, including on civilian and energy targets.
A series of moves by the Trump administration in October raised questions about Washington's reliability as Kyiv's most important military partner.
Tuesday's announcement follows U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff saying late Monday that Washington will mediate Ukraine-Russia peace talks in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11, focusing on security arrangements, de-escalation and humanitarian issues.
Witkoff also said that U.S. negotiators will meet European and NATO officials in Brussels this week to discuss post-war security guarantees and Ukraine's reconstruction.

articles.title_orig: 'Apparently I am afraid of heights': The Peruvian hotel with a terrifying check-in
articles.title_zh: 'Apparently I am afraid of heights': The Peruvian hotel with a terrifying check-in
articles.content_orig:
Suspended 365m above Peru's Sacred Valley, Skylodge's transparent sleeping pods offer extraordinary views – but getting there requires nerves of steel.
My legs quivered as I carefully repositioned my hiking boot on the half-inch braided wire beneath me. Gripping the via ferrata cable near my eyeline, I slipped my carabiner onto the next stretch of metal and took a step out over 200m (656ft) of free air.
"Apparently I am afraid of heights," I shouted behind me to my husband as he too navigated the precarious bridge. With only the cable beneath my feet, the sheer granite cliffs of Peru's Sacred Valley dropped away towards the murky-green Urubamba River far below. I shuffled awkwardly across the 20m (66ft) gap, repeating one instruction to myself: don't look down.
Finally at the other side, I eased myself onto a metal ladder. Our guide, Efren Lopez, assured me we had only a few hundred more metres to climb.
All this was simply the check-in process.
Our destination was Skylodge Adventure Suites , a collection of transparent capsules clinging to a sheer cliff face 365m (1,200ft) above the Sacred Valley floor – navigated via an expertly engineered series of ladders, wire traverses, iron rungs and steps. My husband and I, along with four others, had come to spend a night suspended above the Peruvian Andes.
Once the agricultural heartland of the Inca Empire, Peru's Sacred Valley draws visitors to its Inca ruins, traditional villages and spectacular mountain scenery. The small village of Pachar, where Skylodge is located, is just 10km (6.2 miles) away from the bustling Inca town of Ollantaytambo, but its fertile green floodplains and snow-capped Andean peaks feel worlds away.
Getting there: Skylodge Adventure Suites is approximately 90 minutes from Cusco. Guests reach the capsules via a guided two-hour via ferrata climb and descend via zipline.
How long: Choose between a half-day experience with lunch or a single-night stay.
How much: A one-night stay, including transfers from Cusco, guiding, the via ferrata ascent and zipline descent costs 1,640 Peruvian soles (£350/$480) per person
When to go: The dry season, typically April to October, for prime stargazing.
An easier alternative: The same operator also runs Starlodge Adventure Suites, lower on the cliffside and accessible via a short walk. Its capsules have showers, flushing toilets and an outdoor hot tub for star-gazing soaks.
Lopez led us steadily upwards, negotiating a series of narrow ledges carved into the granite cliff. Pausing on a small platform, barely wide enough for three people, I tightened my safety harness and looked out onto the valley. Far below, the Urubamba River twisted between cultivated fields, framed by sharp peaks.
Still dizzy, I dared to look towards the pods high above. As another climber struggled to squeeze onto the platform, I was nudged onward up the granite cliffside.
Despite my initial trepidation, I gradually found my rhythm, clipping and unclipping the carabiners as we climbed. But the thin mountain air left me wheezing as we crested 3,200m (10,500ft) above sea level, and by the time I finally hauled myself onto the metal platform outside the dining pod, two hours after beginning our ascent, I was exhausted.
Even here, there was little respite for anyone afraid of heights. The capsules seemed to hang over empty space. Only once I was safely inside, free of my harness, could I finally collapse into a chair and breathe.
My husband and I sat with our four climbing companions over a pot of tea, watching the sun set over the Sacred Valley through the dining pod's transparent walls, while our guide, Lopez, prepared a four-course Peruvian dinner. We tucked into pumpkin soup, chicken remoulade and Andean potatoes, followed by a rich cacao brownie topped with fresh maracuyá (passionfruit). Outside, the pink sky gradually darkened, revealing the first stars and the turbid spray of the Milky Way.
I downed the remainder of my wine in a single gulp as I remembered that reaching our bedroom would require another climb.
Lopez helped us back into our harnesses and clipped us in for the short ascent to our private pods. Using iron hand- and foot-grips drilled into the granite, my husband and I climbed towards our bedroom, where we'd remain until morning.
"Be sure to stay up late for the best views of the Milky Way," he reminded us.
Clinging to the cliff face, our sleeping pod was reached through a hatch in the roof. Inside were three beds – a double and two singles – and six windows offering views across the Sacred Valley. The bathroom was decidedly less luxurious: an ecologically friendly "dry" toilet, separated from the rest of the pod by a thick curtain, with no shower in sight.
• No cars, no phone signal: Canada's ghost island where guests still check in
• An icy 4,554m hike to Europe's highest overnight stay
• A stay in Pakistan's remote Ishkoman Valley, where humans still consult fairies
The temperature dropped quickly inside the pod and I curled up on the double bed beneath a pile of thick blankets, peering through the curved wall. There was little to do but read, sip wine and wait for the darkest hour and brightest stars. I listened to the faint sounds of civilisation drifting up the mountain from the road below: the occasional car horn, a distant siren and the rattle of wind whipping against the pod's exterior.
Earlier that evening, Lopez had explained the importance of the night sky in Inca culture. "The Urubamba River below us was viewed by the Incas as the earthly mirror of the Milky Way, and every living being had a celestial counterpart in the picturesque galaxy," he told us.
Now, lying high above the valley, I gazed up at the Milky Way while its earthly counterpart wound through the valley below. As the sky erupted with even more stars, I felt as though I was drifting to sleep among them, not beneath them.
Just before 06:00, golden morning light flooded my pod. Outside, birdsong echoed across the valley as the other guests began to stir.
After scuttling our way back to the dining pod for breakfast, we prepared for our final adventure: a descent along six ziplines, ranging from 150m (490ft) to 700m (2,300ft) in length. Clipping into the first line with confidence, I stole one last glance at the rugged hillside. I had finally found my sea legs up here.
Pushing off the platform, I hurtled between orange granite spires towards Lopez, who was waiting in the distance. Just before reaching the end of the line, I leaned right, avoiding a sharp whack as the automatic brake caught, helping me to drift lightly onto the next landing.
I careened from platform to platform, zig zagging down the cliff, lowering myself closer to the valley floor with each slide. Less than an hour later, I was back on solid ground.
The experience had been more challenging than any of us had imagined. But after a night suspended above the Sacred Valley, the quiet of nature, the deep satisfaction of enduring a physical challenge and the spectacular views had me fantasising about a future filled with climbs and cliffside camps.

articles.title_orig: Shopify Stock Plunges As Q3 Gross Operating Profit, Revenue Miss
articles.title_zh: Shopify Stock Plunges As Q3 Gross Operating Profit, Revenue Miss
articles.content_orig:
Shares of e-commerce platform Shopify fell 7% on Tuesday after the company missed estimates on subscription gross profit and gross merchandise volume.
Shopify reported before the bell Tuesday and posted adjusted earnings of 49 cents per share, topping LSEG estimates of 46 cents per share.
Overall, quarterly revenue of $3.74 billion came in just below LSEG estimates of $3.75 billion. Shopify said it sees revenue growth in the "low thirties" range year over year for the fourth quarter, versus LSEG estimates of 32.1%.
Gross merchandise volume, which came in at $119.15 billion, missed analyst estimates of $120.03 billion for the quarter, according to StreetAccount. Subscription gross profit also missed estimates by nearly $20 million, coming in at $661 million compared to StreetAccount estimates of $680.3 million. Merchant gross profit beat estimates.
Shopify president Harley Finkelstein called the GMV results "consistent" and "durable" in comments to CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Tuesday, and noted it was the thirteenth consecutive quarter of GMV growth above 20%.
"We're really proud of the print, and we're going to keep building for the long term and ignore the noise day to day," Finkelstein said.
Subscription revenue of $836 million also missed analyst estimates of $848.1 million, according to FactSet. Merchant revenue beat estimates.

articles.title_orig: King to open Commonwealth summit as Burnham begins talks on slavery apology
articles.title_zh: King to open Commonwealth summit as Burnham begins talks on slavery apology
articles.content_orig:
Speech by Charles marks formal opening of Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm) in Antigua
Charles carries on with his remarks about history. (See 2.50pm .) Turning to the slave trade, he does not issue an apology – but he says slavery history “fills my heart with horror”, and he stresses the importance of addressing the “wrongs of the past”.
double quotation mark Our history inspires us, can appal us, yet it can always teach us. We cannot change the actions of those who came before us. We can, however, learn from the past.
The transatlantic trade in enslaved persons still casts a shadow over these islands, and other members of our Commonwealth.
As I have said before, that shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow.
And yet, history also teaches us that evil need not have the last word, that character and courage can combine to overcome the most monstrous injustice, as they did with the determination to end the international trade in enslaved people, in which the Royal Navy played such a leading role.
The more I have furthered my own understanding of the issues through listening, learning and looking, the more committed I have become to finding ways for us to work in modern partnership to address the wrongs of the past – with action for the future through improving access to education, investing in jobs and opportunities, encouraging intra-commonwealth trade, and inspiring vital climate resilience measures across the world.
I have always felt that there is so much that can be done to help lift up those who struggle against hardship and disadvantage.
I have always tried to play my part in doing just that. For as any sailor navigating the seas knows, we cannot command the winds, least of all where the winds of yesterday have delivered us. But we can choose how we set our sails.
The British and Australian governments have backed a joint agreement at the Commonwealth summit on working together to tackle threats directed at parliamentarians, especially women. Here is an extract.
double quotation mark We commit to working together with the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association, with the Commonwealth Women Parliamentarians, and with countries from across the Commonwealth to bring together technology, expertise and practical solutions to help protect parliamentarians from online abuse and support democratic participation across the Commonwealth. We’ll hold the first forum in 2027 and will engage all those in the Commonwealth who share these values.
There are a range of software tools that are being trialled in our parliaments and around the world, and we welcome and encourage this innovation.
While we work to change attitudes, restore respectful debate and return people’s choice, in the short term we can commit to take steps together to protect our democracies.
Severin Carrell is the Guardian’s Scotland editor.
MSPs at Holyrood have called on Scottish ministers to review a law which allowed the Indian-born student Q Manivannan to win a seat at Holyrood in May, claiming public confidence in parliament was “fragile”.
The standards, procedures and public appointments committee said in a report that the rationale for allowing people with limited rights to be in the UK was “simply not clear” and had “run ahead of what the public want”.
Under the Scottish Elections (Representation and Reform) Act 2025, overseas citizens with the legal right to live in Scotland can stand for Holyrood and local councils, even if their rights are temporary.
There was an outcry led by the Conservatives and Reform UK in May when Manivannan was elected as a Scottish Greens list MSP for Edinburgh and Lothians East. A successful PhD candidate at St Andrews, it emerged their student visa was due to expire at the end of 2026. They have since been granted a three-year graduate visa, giving them right to remain until the end of 2029.
Jenny Minto , the Scottish National party MSP who chairs the committee, and who voted in favour of the reforms last year, said public sentiment appears to have swung against the policy. She said:
double quotation mark It is vital that Scotland has elected representatives who look like the communities they represent. This diversity helps build trust in our elected institutions.
But we know that this trust is fragile, and so careful consideration needs to be given to all electoral reform that comes before us.
Reform UK was delighted by the committee’s recommendation, which follows proposals by ministers to extend the right to Commonwealth citizens, but the Scottish Greens said it was regressive. The Scottish Greens said:
double quotation mark There are thousands of people with limited leave to remain who live and work in Scotland and have made a home here, including Commonwealth citizens. They should be able to stand for our parliament and councils.
MSPs backed this change unanimously at the time, including the convenor and deputy convenor of the committee. It would be a regrettable backwards step for representation and democracy if Scotland was to roll back on this commitment.
Andy Burnham has said that he cares less about what the newspapers say about him than previous prime ministers did.
In one of his interviews with Daniel Hewitt for the ITV documentary being shown tonight about his first 100 days in office, Burnham was asked if he cared less about what papers like the Daily Mail and the Sun said about him than some of his predecessors did. Burnham replied: “Definitely.”
double quotation mark I left Westminster for a reason. I got fed up with commentators deciding things down there and then the whole world [being] meant to believe what they believe. Well, sorry, the world’s not like that anymore.
Burnham also defended prioritising social media more instead. He said:
double quotation mark People want more involvement, more understanding of the way politics is being done and that’s what I’m bringing. And hopefully it connects with people, particularly younger people, who may have felt quite distant from politics.
In another interview for the programme, Burnham rejected the suggestion that he was ruthless. Explaining why he did not like the description, he said:
double quotation mark Determined, I definitely would say that [I am] determined. I will come back and back and back at something. I’ve always been like that. Ruthless to me says you just have a disregard for everybody else. And that wouldn’t be me. But I am determined.
Burnham also revealed that, since becoming PM, he continues to go running regularly – and that this is often when his “best thoughts” occur. He explained:
double quotation mark If you’re asking me about what’s the thing that makes it work, I go running and I’ve not stopped my running. It’s when my mind goes a bit into neutral. And I feel then I get my best thoughts in those moments.
You know, all of a sudden, "Oh, that, yeah, I’ll do that.’ Or a particularly intractable problem that you’ve been thinking and worrying about – all of a sudden, I’ve been out on a run sometimes, and you just think, ‘Ah, that’s the way I’ll go into that one.’

articles.content_orig:
You have got to wait another couple of weeks to gain access to the official set of new PS Plus Premium games for this month, but in the meantime, there's been a bonus addition to the service.
Not announced or highlighted by Sony or publisher Deep Silver, the new PS5 version of Metro Redux — which improves and enhances Metro 2033 and Metro: Last Light — has been added to PS Plus Premium. The old PS4 version was on there already, but now the listing has been updated to support the PS5 edition too.
This new PS5 version brings significant improvements over the original PS4 bundle of the two intense shooters, so they are worth revisiting again if you haven't already. Here's what to expect on PS5:
The third game in the series, Metro Exodus , was added to PS Plus Extra a few months ago, so now the entire franchise is playable natively on PS5 through Sony's subscription service. Now would also be a great time to catch up, with Metro 2039 out in February 2027.
Will you use PS Plus as a way to play through the Metro games for the first time, or do you fancy revisiting any of them? Let us know in the comments below.
[source store.playstation.com ]
Liam grew up with a PlayStation controller in his hands and a love for Metal Gear Solid. Nowadays, he's found playing the latest and greatest PS5 games as well as supporting Derby County. That last detail is his downfall.
That’s nice. Fantastic way to enjoy these titles.
I bought both of those games on PS4 so I snagged the free PS5 upgrades instead
I've never got round to playing any of the Metro games but I've heard great things. I don't do horror, how much do they lean into that or is it more of a focus on the story and world than straight-up scares?
Cool. Nice of them to double pack.
@springer17 I can't handle scares all that much and I never felt frightened of the series, mind you I've read the novels too and they are more terrifying because it relies on the readers imagination. Think of it more like how Fallout approaches it's combat/story beats. I'd call it more psychological and existential. For me the Horror was in the reality it's my city, for others I've talked to it's the claustrophobia. But the kind of scares that jump from Western studios isn't something you have to worry about. It's built differently is what I'm trying to say, I would call the games technical achievements even before those upgrades. You should definitely give them a try if you have the time.
I was actually thinking about playing these more recently so might finally be a good time to sign up for PS+ again for a month and knock them out.

great games - paid full price for them back in the day - might go revisit them before the new one is out in Dec

articles.title_orig: Binance founder Changpeng Zhao addresses historic crypto hack: 'There's no 100% security'
articles.title_zh: Binance founder Changpeng Zhao addresses historic crypto hack: 'There's no 100% security'
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
It has been a busy few days for Changpeng Zhao in the wake of the hack on the enormous crypto platform he co-founded, Binance.
"It's been a pretty hectic process," Zhao, better known in crypto circles as CZ , told Yahoo Finance. "But the good thing is right now the withdrawals have been restored, the systems back to normal. People are free to use the platform without any issues now. And then all user funds are covered. The users did not suffer any loss."
Binance is the world's largest cryptocurrency trading platform and holds approximately $171 billion in total assets on its platform. The company is led by co-CEOs Richard Teng and Yi Le.
Hackers recently drained roughly $6.3 billion worth of digital assets from Binance on Oct. 29.
Here's what you need to know:
Blockchain intelligence firms and the FBI attributed the 20-minute raid with high confidence to TraderTraitor, an elite state-sponsored cyber unit tied to North Korea.
North Korea reportedly denied involvement.
Rather than cracking private cryptographic keys, the attackers reportedly breached internal automated transaction workflows via a Binance employee's laptop.
Read more: How to keep your crypto safe
Binance moved swiftly to stabilize the situation by guaranteeing full customer restitution, deploying corporate treasury reserves, Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) capital, and insurance funds to replenish user balances.
"There's no 100% security," CZ added. "So when you run a platform, especially a crypto platform the possibility is always there. I did not think it was going to be this big of magnitude, probably not."

articles.title_orig: Premier Tusk Says Poland Foiled Possible Provocation at Russia Border
articles.title_zh: Premier Tusk Says Poland Foiled Possible Provocation at Russia Border
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Poland has thwarted a potential Russian “provocation” on its border, according to the country’s prime minister Donald Tusk .
Tensions have been mounting between the countries over a series of issues including airspace violations and diplomatic disagreements as Europe remains concerned about a wider escalation from Moscow.
On Tuesday Polish police units were sent to the country’s border with the Russian enclave of Kaliningrad , Tusk said.
“We managed to prevent attempts at provocation – if that was indeed the intention,” he told reporters, according to France24.
He said that “individuals with flashlights” had been observed in the area, sparking concern.
“Just after midnight, I received information from the border guards that disturbing movement had been observed on the Polish-Russian border,” he said.
“We very quickly mobilised the appropriate forces and resources there and managed to prevent a provocation.”
The military, border guards and intelligence services had already been carrying out additional activities in the area to strengthen security.
A police spokesperson said that these preventive measures had been conducted in the northeastern regions of Warmia-Masuria and Podlaskie.
When authorities received “more precise” information about acts of sabotage including a potential incursion into Poland by “armed people” in the first half of November, additional police and troops were deployed as part of a special operation along the border regions on Tuesday, Tusk said.
“We have been receiving information for some time from our services and from allies' services that ... acts of diversion or more serious provocations on the border with Russia , or even sabotage acts orchestrated by hostile services, could occur,” he explained.
The Polish leader said he had also received warnings about possible escalations from Nato ’s supreme allied commander in Europe during his visit to Warsaw in October.
Tusk also accused Russia of trying to foment “instability” in Poland by meddling in a dispute between the government and the president over the Constitutional Tribunal.
President Karol Naworcki and Tusk have butted heads over the Tribunal leading to the suspension of the head of the court last week.
Russian politicians including Dmitry Medvedev, the deputy chairman of Russia's Security Council, described Tusk’s government's moves in the dispute as “a coup”.
“We observe activity by Russia and pro-Russian politicians —both internationally and within the country, centring around our cause, which is defending the Constitutional Tribunal against aggressive behaviour by politicians and the demonstrators they provoke,” he said.
“We are all familiar with the Russian method of becoming involved in internal conflicts. Today, we are witnessing tensions provoked by the Russians, whether in connection with the midterm elections (in the US) or through the fuelling of a sense of instability (in Poland), based on the aggressive behaviour of opposition politicians and the president.”

articles.title_orig: Yum Brands earnings beat estimates, but cyclospora outbreak weighs on Taco Bell
articles.title_zh: Yum Brands earnings beat estimates, but cyclospora outbreak weighs on Taco Bell
articles.content_orig:
Yum Brands on Tuesday reported earnings that beat expectations, but a cyclospora outbreak linked to iceberg lettuce at Taco Bell weighed on the company's same-store sales growth.
However, Yum said Taco Bell, which the company considers a "growth engine" for its business, has since rebounded.
"Since the end of September, Taco Bell U.S. has been outpacing the [quick-service restaurant] industry on same-store sales growth," Yum CEO Chris Turner said in a statement.
Taco Bell's same-store sales are up about 1% so far in the fourth quarter, CFO Ranjith Roy said on the company's earnings conference call Tuesday. In the last four weeks ended Friday, same-store sales have risen 3% compared with the year-ago period.
Here's what the company reported compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
Yum reported fiscal third-quarter net income of $1.62 billion, or $5.92 per share, up from $397 million, or $1.41 per share, a year earlier.
Excluding gains from its divestiture of Pizza Hut and other items, the restaurant company earned $1.56 per share.
Net sales rose 4% to $2.05 billion.
During the quarter, Yum completed its divestiture of Pizza Hut. It closed the sale of the pizza chain's business in mainland China to Yum China on Aug. 7 and sold the rest of Pizza Hut to LongRange Capital on Sept. 1. The company's third-quarter results include Pizza Hut up until those dates.
Excluding Pizza Hut, Yum's same-store sales were flat for the quarter as Taco Bell weighed on the company's overall results. Taco Bell's same-store sales declined by 4% as diners temporarily pulled back on visits due to the foodborne illness outbreak .
Yum executives previously said the weekend of July 18 saw the most severe impact to sales, but trends have improved since then.
Taco Bell's most loyal customers returned faster, Yum said, thanks in part to weekly Tuesday deals for loyalty program members after the cyclospora outbreak took over headlines.
Traffic from "medium" and "light" customers has bounced back to about 95% of prior levels, while visits from "heavy" users is back to normal, Roy said. To attract more casual diners, Taco Bell has been relying on star power, like a collaboration with pop star Olivia Rodrigo on a pink-colored Mountain Dew Baja Blast.
Outside of the U.S., Taco Bell's much smaller international business reported same-store sales growth of 5%.
KFC's same-store sales ticked up 1%, helped by system sales growth in China and Europe. The U.S., now the chicken chain's third-largest market, saw system sales shrink 6% in the quarter.
Like Restaurant Brands International's Popeyes , KFC has struggled in the U.S. amid a wave of new competitors and more budget-conscious consumers. Its home market represents only about 5% of KFC's operating profit, but it remains a symbolically important part of the business for Yum investors.
During the quarter, KFC U.S. launched popcorn chicken, which sold out in many restaurants. However, Yum said the limited-time menu item was not enough to offset the successful Hot & Spicy Wings and Potato Wedges promotion during the year-ago period.
Globally, KFC is trying to become "the most modern chicken QSR ," Turner said on the company's earnings conference call. To achieve that lofty goal, he said the chain will roll out buzzy promotions, a new brand identity, and a wider menu that includes upgraded sauces and more beverages.

articles.title_orig: Midterm elections could jolt stocks if Democrats sweep Congress
articles.title_zh: Midterm elections could jolt stocks if Democrats sweep Congress
articles.content_orig:
The stock market is not yet pricing in a Democratic sweep of Congress — despite some polls and most prediction markets pointing that way — so that scenario could weigh on share prices Wednesday, according to investors and analysts.
Republicans managing to keep control could cause a short-term relief rally, they said.
Short-term moves aside, the typical post-midterm pattern in the months ahead is bullish. But some wonder if the market could buck the positive historical trend this time because the S&P 500 is already up so much this year going into the election.
As far as certain stocks to watch, a big Democratic win on Tuesday night — especially in the Texas governor race — could add fuel to an artificial intelligence stock sell-off on the notion that more data center restrictions would gain momentum nationally. Defense stocks could come under pressure on fears of limits on spending.
Polls are pointing to a Democratic victory in the House and a toss-up in the Senate. Prediction markets have been more favorable to Democrats, calling for a blue sweep .
While investors are signaling "begrudging acceptance" to a base-case scenario that there will indeed be a Democratic sweep, that's not how they're positioning, said Tobin Marcus, head of U.S. policy and politics at Wolfe Research. The firm's recent survey data among more than 100 institutional investors suggests they are not strongly positioned for any particular result.
"Investors seem to have a significant dose of skepticism about whether the final outcome is going to be quite as favorable to Democrats as the polling suggests," Marcus told CNBC, noting that the firm shares the view that the "polling is likely overstating Democratic strength."
JPMorgan sees a blue wave knocking the S&P 500 by about a half percent on Wednesday.
On the other hand, if Republicans end up retaining both chambers of Congress, that could spur a rally, said Sameer Samana, head of global equities and real assets at the Wells Fargo Investment Institute.
"From a certainty standpoint, the market knows what to do with Republicans holding both chambers," he said.
Citigroup strategists said Monday that Republicans losing the House but managing to keep the Senate could be "a tailwind for equities into year-end." JPMorgan traders predict up to a 1% pop on Wednesday if Republicans hold on to that chamber.
Looking past any short-term move, stocks tend to rally after the midterms have concluded. In fact, the S&P 500 was up one year out after all midterm elections going back to the early 1980s.
But the S&P 500 has already recorded double-digit gains so far in 2026, so some on Wall Street worry that investors are being overly complacent heading into this year's elections.
During midterm election years, the S&P 500 has typically averaged a 14% drawdown at some point in the second half of the year found Jonathan Krinsky, chief market technician at BTIG.
"The reason stocks often perform well in November during midterms is because [the S&P 500] typically is weak INTO the elections. We have the opposite setup this year," Krinsky wrote last week. "Therefore, while consensus is that we see a post midterm rally, we think the opposite is actually more likely."
It's not helping that the broader market has recently come under significant pressure due to turbulence in the artificial intelligence trade, which led the Nasdaq Composite to post its worst day since June on Friday. AI shares led the market lower again on Monday.
A strong showing from Democrats in Tuesday's midterm elections could pressure the trade even more .
At the state level, increased Democratic control is probably a headwind for stocks associated with data centers and technological capital equipment, analysts said.
"It [would solidify] the early kind of cautionary signs in different states around the advancement of AI infrastructure," Rob Rains at Washington Analysis told CNBC.
Goldman Sachs strategists said this week that a Democratic Congress "might limit data center tax incentives, but a national moratorium looks unlikely in any election outcome."
One example would be Texas — a key hub of the data center buildout. A surprise loss there by Republican Gov. Greg Abbott has the "potential to spook" the market in the short term, Wolfe's Marcus said.
A blue wave might pressure defense shares, while boosting healthcare stocks, analysts and investors said.
"A substantial Democratic sweep could limit real spending growth unless a broader agreement increases both defense and health-care funding," said Alex Sagal, global equity analyst at Wells Fargo Investment Institute. However, he noted that the earnings outlook for the defense industry looks "stable to modestly positive."
Wolfe Research's Marcus said that healthcare is going to be "the biggest focus," as Democrats will push for restoring expired Affordable Care Act enhanced premium subsidies or unwinding some of the Medicaid reforms in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act .
"Healthcare stocks have been doing really well lately," Jed Ellerbroek, portfolio manager at Argent Capital Management, said to CNBC. "I think part of that is the anti-AI trade, but I also think part of it is just optimism that Democrats are taking over."
Ellerbroek is keeping his eye on hospital-related stocks such as HCA Healthcare and Tenet Healthcare as well as health insurers like UnitedHealth and Centene .
Financials was the worst S&P 500 sector in early 2026 on the heels of President Donald Trump calling on Congress to pass a law that would cap credit card interest rates at 10% . While the sector has been able to notch gains since, with its year-to-date rise now at around 3%, things could get more unstable for the group under Democratic control.
"Democrats will come in wanting to show tangible progress on the affordability issue, and that means targeting sectors that are front and center in consumer budgets," said Evercore ISI's Matthew Aks. "We know Trump has populist instincts, populist leanings, and could he pick a couple of issues and decide to team up with the Democrats on those issues and target those industries in a populist way? Absolutely."
Given that Democratic control is often associated with increased regulation, while Republican control is thought to promote deregulation, Democrats could be interested in passing credit card rate caps if they come out victorious.
"I think if Democrats have control of one or both chambers, they would try to pass it and see if they could get Trump to either sign it or force him to veto it, and that would let Democrats kind of score a political point," Aks said.
Trump could restart the war against Iran after holding off on any major strikes leading up to the midterms, a move that could upend the overall market and cause energy stocks to outperform. Crude oil prices jumped more than 10% in October, though they gave a lot of that gain back on Monday.
Gasoline prices stood at $4.17 a gallon on average nationwide Sunday, a nearly 40% increase compared with the same period last year, according to AAA.
"If there are escalations, that could obviously put upward pressure on prices just ahead of Thanksgiving," said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at Gas Buddy, "which is also when Americans have really staunch traditions in terms of driving to friends and family."
If Trump decides to take forceful action, it could snuff out hope for a typical post-midterm year-end rally.
Evercore ISI said the S&P 500 could retreat by double digits to end the year at 6,800 as oil spikes if the president "moves to kinetic escalation in Iran ahead of seating the new Congress in January" and Democrats take Congress.
— With reporting by Sarah Min, Tobias Burns and Spencer Kimball.

articles.title_orig: Smugglers Bypass U.S. Controls to Ship HBM to China
articles.title_zh: Smugglers Bypass U.S. Controls to Ship HBM to China
articles.content_orig:
Despite U.S. export controls on advanced semiconductors to China, High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) produced by Samsung Electronics and SK hynix is reportedly being smuggled into China. Smugglers are using a method of packaging HBMs with low-end server processors to bypass export regulations, and then detaching only the memory once in China.
According to the U.S. IT media outlet The Information on Nov. 2 (local time), smugglers who have recently been siphoning Korean HBMs to China are exploiting loopholes in export regulations.
They package the HBM with a low-end server processor on a board and export it to China. They target the fact that while exporting HBM alone is subject to U.S. regulations, packaging it with a server processor classifies the package as a server processor item.
Under U.S. export regulations, the total computing power of a semiconductor package is evaluated based on the server processor, not the memory chip. The packages are disassembled upon arriving in China. Local technicians apply heat to the board to melt the solder, detach only the necessary HBM, and discard the remaining server processors.
The separation process requires highly sophisticated skills. It is reported that the failure rate is high because applying heat too quickly or for an extended period can cause the memory stack to warp or crack.
Nevertheless, the smuggling continues due to the massive profits.
A broker in his 20s who handles HBM smuggling in China told The Information that the price of a single HBM3E, which traded for several hundred dollars just a year ago, has recently soared to about $4,000. A single AI chip package requires 6 to 8 HBMs. The memory price alone amounts to $24,000 to $32,000. AI processors, servers, and power costs are separate.
The HBMs secured in this way are reportedly sold mainly to customers of Huawei, a Chinese telecommunications equipment and IT company.
According to sources familiar with Huawei’s supply chain, Huawei recently explained to some customers that its next-generation flagship AI chip, the Ascend 960DT, will largely be equipped with HBMs produced by Samsung Electronics and SK hynix. Huawei introduced that the performance of the Ascend 960DT is twice as superior as existing chips, and it will be one of the powerful processors that China can produce on its own.
As it became difficult to directly purchase the necessary memory chips from Korean companies, Huawei even advised some AI chip ordering customers to secure HBMs on their own. China is clinging to securing Korean HBMs because it lacks its own production capacity.
HBM is a core component that enhances the processing performance of AI processors by quickly transmitting large amounts of data. Without securing enough HBMs, it is difficult for a high-performance AI chip to exert its full performance even if it is developed. Samsung Electronics and SK hynix account for more than 80% of the global HBM market.
The problem is that such smuggling could also act as a burden on Korean semiconductor companies. Even if Samsung Electronics and SK hynix did not directly violate export control regulations, they could become targets of U.S. government surveillance if Chinese AI chips equipped with their memory are discovered.
In fact, Taiwan’s TSMC was investigated by the U.S. government in 2024 after semiconductors it produced were found in Huawei products. Subsequently, the U.S. ordered TSMC to completely halt AI chip exports to China.
SK hynix stated, “We are strictly complying with relevant laws and regulations, including the export control regulations of the U.S. and South Korea,” adding that it has never supplied products to Huawei since the implementation of U.S. export regulations in 2020.
Meanwhile, a perception is emerging among smugglers who consider their transactions to be a patriotic act.
A broker in his 20s who smuggles memory in China told The Information regarding his work, “It is contributing to the motherland.” He reportedly does not consider himself a smuggler.
However, as smuggling competition intensifies, concerns about crackdowns are also growing.
Another smuggler who has been ordering memory semiconductors from South Korea revealed that the risk of detection is increasing as other brokers have started using the transaction routes he used.
He said, “The more people like us there are, the easier it becomes to be discovered by regulatory authorities,” adding that he plans to sell most of his company stakes next year as crackdowns by South Korea and the U.S. are expected to be further strengthened in the future.

articles.title_orig: Labour MPs pull their punches on immigration changes
articles.title_zh: Labour MPs pull their punches on immigration changes
articles.content_orig:
Today's announcement has long been viewed in government as a potential political banana skin.
When the home secretary announced her first version of changes to the settlement system last year, many Labour MPs, including the housing secretary Angela Rayner, voiced their concerns about the plans.
But there was a feeling that Sir Keir Starmer's government was determined to plough on regardless. Shabana Mahmood herself repeatedly expressed how important she believed the reforms were.
But the change of prime minister over the summer gave renewed hope to those unhappy Labour MPs that they could force the Home Office into two changes.
Firstly, social care workers – under the original plans many social care workers would have had to wait 15 years before becoming eligible for settlement.
Secondly, the retrospective nature of the plans – some MPs were uncomfortable at the idea of someone coming to the UK and expecting to be eligible for settlement after five years, but then having to wait longer.
Angela Rayner described that as "un-British" and said the government shouldn't be shifting "the goalposts".
She returned to the cabinet under Andy Burnham as housing secretary and chose to repeat those criticisms in an interview during the Labour Party conference in September.
That was seen as evidence that a debate inside the top levels of government about whether to water down the plans was well and truly rumbling on.
For all the Labour MPs who wanted a change, there were others, particularly those in Brexit-supporting areas, who wanted the home secretary to stick the course.
Some inside government felt nervous about providing what they saw as catnip to Reform and the Conservatives.
All of that added up to one of the more difficult decisions that has had to be taken since Burnham walked through the doors of Number 10.
In the end ministers chose to water down the proposals for care workers – those who arrived before May 2025 and earn at least £25,000 a year will qualify for settlement in five years.
But the retrospective nature of the plans, the thing Rayner described as shifting "the goalposts", hasn't changed.
Despite that, the majority of Labour MPs pulled their punches when Mahmood made a statement in the House of Commons earlier .
Perhaps the strongest pushback came from Rachael Maskell, who is no fan of the retrospective element - but others on the left of the party, including John McDonnell and Diane Abbott, were critical without being scathing.
Outside the Commons chamber, the mood among Labour folk was pretty similar to what was said from the green benches.
One would-be critic said that while they personally still had concerns about the plans announced today, they believed the Home Secretary had successfully taken the political sting out of the situation for now.
They said the campaign by MPs and unions had led to a "big win" on settlement for social care workers, but said they were still expecting to hear from constituents negatively affected by the new rules.
One Number 10 source praised Mahmood's "take no prisoners" performance in the chamber, argued she had "found the right balance" and said the announcement had gone down as well as could be expected with Labour colleagues.
Of course, the home secretary will still need to deal with criticism from other parties.
Her opposite number for the Conservatives, Chris Philp, accused Mahmood of a significant U-turn.
Philp highlighted a claim she had previously made – that allowing care workers to reach settlement more quickly could cost the UK £10bn.
The social care workers plans announced today will see around 500,000 people have their path to settlement delayed , that number would have been around 800,000 under the original plans last year.
In an interview with the BBC, Mahmood wouldn't say what sort of financial burden her watering down would result in.
She also refused to confirm whether Burnham had directly asked her to water down the plans.
They are tricky questions that she will have to navigate over the coming weeks.
But the general view within government is that this is one political hurdle that has been successfully jumped.

articles.title_orig: US, Russia and China discuss trilateral meeting between Trump, Putin and Xi
articles.title_zh: US, Russia and China discuss trilateral meeting between Trump, Putin and Xi
articles.content_orig:
Fox News chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst reports on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's response to Russian attacks, warning that strikes on their infrastructure will meet a painful response.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned Monday that Russia is preparing a "massive attack" on Ukraine centered on Tuesday's midterm elections in the United States, accusing Moscow of seeking to exploit the historical vote to unleash strikes while the world's attention is elsewhere.
The Ukrainian leader's warning came as voters prepared to decide which party controls Congress, a result that could also influence Washington's future response to Russian President Vladimir Putin's almost five-year war in Ukraine.
In a post on X, Zelenskyy went on to urge the Trump administration to increase pressure on Moscow, warning that Russia could exploit the elections to target Ukraine's battered energy infrastructure and supply routes.
DRONE STRIKE SINKS SHIP IN NATO WATERS AS ZELENSKYY WARNS OF LOOMING ‘MASSIVE STRIKE’
Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. (Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Sputnik/Kremlin Pool Photo/Efrem Lukatsky/AP)
"We have intel that Russia is preparing a new massive attack on our country – primarily targeting energy and logistics," Zelenskyy said in his nightly address.
"The assumption is basically that tomorrow the world will be watching the American midterms, and what is happening here in Ukraine, along with our difficulties with air defense and Patriot missiles, will be overlooked."
Zelenskyy's warning came hours after Russian forces struck a school being used to distribute humanitarian aid in Komyshuvakha, a settlement in southeastern Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region.
At least 26 people, including police officers and first responders, were killed, five others were injured and others remained missing, according to the Ukrainian news outlet Ukrainska Pravda .
ZELENSKYY PRESSURES US AND EUROPE FOR MORE 'AIR DEFENSE' ASSISTANCE AMID ONGOING WAR WITH RUSSIA
Ukraine's largest private energy company reports 90% of generation capacity damaged by Russian attacks, leaving over 1 million without power during freezing temperatures. (Reuters)
In his X post, Zelenskyy urged the U.S. and its allies to warn Putin that continued attacks on Ukraine would bring serious economic consequences.
"We need signals from the world to Russia that will make them feel that terror is no good, that it will bring no gains, and that as long as this war continues, their oil will burn, and they will not be able to make money doing business with the world," Zelenskyy warned.
"We must not play games with Russia's oil or gas revenues," he added.
"We must put pressure on Russia in such a way that it has no alternative but to end this war. America can do this."
TRUMP ANNOUNCES IMMEDIATE ENERGY CEASEFIRE BETWEEN RUSSIA AND UKRAINE
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, left talks with President Donald Trump and members of his Cabinet during a lunch meeting at the White House on Oct. 17, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
President Donald Trump, meanwhile, has sought to negotiate an end to the war with the help of special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner , both of whom have been involved in diplomatic efforts with Moscow.
Zelenskyy told Fox News in a Sunday interview that Ukraine would suspend strikes on Russian oil refineries for a month if Washington provided Patriot missile interceptors during the same period, potentially opening the door to diplomacy.
The State Department approved the potential sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 interceptor missiles to Ukraine for an estimated $2.1 billion, according to Reuters.
The proposed sale could provide a significant boost to Ukraine's air defenses if finalized, although the delivery timeline is uncertain.
TRUMP SAYS US WILL LET UKRAINE MAKE PATRIOT MISSILES IN MAJOR POLICY SHIFT
